newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's TranzRail freight volumes hit by economy, NZ$.
newsitem.headline: NZ's TranzRail freight volumes hit by economy, NZ$.

text.p: The chairman of New Zealand rail operator Tranz Rail Holdings Ltd (TRH) said on Wednesday that key parts of its core bulk freight carryings in New Zealand were being hit by general weakness in the economy and the strong kiwi dollar that in turn cut export volumes.

Ed Burkhardt, who represents TRH's largest owner, U.S. rail freight group Wisconsin Central Transportation Corp , told Reuters in an interview that the cargo volume fall "held our business at year-ago levels" by offsetting some growth experienced in the business during recent months.
TRH is due to report third quarter results in early May.
"We're seeing some weaknesses in those (core freight) areas which we're overcoming by efforts on the operating cost side," Burkhardt said.
The TRH chairman, in Wellington for a routine board meeting, said of freight volume, "It's being held down right now a bit because of general weakness in the economy."
Asked where the impact of the New Zealand dollar's strength was being felt he said it was hitting coal, dairy and meat "...and forestry products are particulary weak just now".
He said the net effect on the company's total freight volume was probably nil, as it cancelled out organic growth.

"I think it has actually held our business at about the year-ago level, which in these circumstances I consider a success, and it's better than the average New Zealand company has done that's active in these areas.
"What's it has done is it's taken the growth away, which I think is temporary," Burkhardt added.

In the six months to December 31, 1996, Tranz Rail's freight volume rose by 12 percent when it moved a record 5.6 million tonnes. Net profit rose about 27.5 percent to NZ$24.1 million ($16.5 million).
Burkhardt declined to comment on current numbers or profits, but said TRH still wanted to increase its freight market share.
Currently the company has about a 20 percent share of total inter-city freight traffic in New Zealand, he estimated.

"These (heavy export commodity) industries which are having problems in their own markets -- they'll all come back. In fact we're looking for a greater penetration or market share of what they're doing," Burkhardt added.
For example, he said, TRH was pushing ahead with bids to carry more raw materials for the export industry such as an ongoing start-up project to haul milk for dairy processors.
"We've ordered tank wagons for a train that will start up in the next few months on the North Island for Kiwi Dairies."

Burkhardt said he did not share the fears expressed in some recent press reports that a plan under study by Solid Energy (formerly Coal Corp of New Zealand) would lead to a collapse in TRH's coal traffic on the South Island.
Solid Energy is reportedly considering building a new deepwater loading jetty near its mines which would make a longhaul rail link to Lyttleton redundant if it went ahead.
"I don't think the jetty will be built. It's a huge investment... it would have be backed up by a much stronger contract position for selling coal than they have right now."
